item.title: Mount Yoshino: Japan's Greatest Cherry-Blossom Mountain — Guide
item.description: Mount Yoshino (Yoshinoyama), in southern Nara, is celebrated as the greatest cherry-blossom destination in all of Japan: some 30,000 cherry trees, planted over more than a thousand years as sacred offerings, cover its slopes and bloom each spring in staggered waves that climb the mountain from the Shimo (lower) grove to the Oku (upper) grove over about two weeks. The effect — whole ridgelines washed in shifting pink, dotted with temples and shrines — is breathtaking, and the mountain is also a sacred centre of Shugendo mountain asceticism and part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

item.title: Tsuruma Park: Nagoya's Great Hanami Gathering — Guide
item.description: Tsuruma Park, opened in 1909 as Nagoya’s first public park, is the city’s great hanami stage: some 700 cherry trees, mostly clouds of Somei-Yoshino, bloom in late March and early April over a gracious landscape of fountains, a Western-style rose garden and a Japanese garden. This is where Nagoya comes to celebrate spring in earnest — blue tarpaulins and office parties pack the lawns by mid-morning, food stalls line the paths, and after dark lanterns and lights turn the central avenues into glowing tunnels of blossom for yozakura night viewing.

item.title: Matsumoto Castle: Japan's Oldest Five-Tiered Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Matsumoto Castle, nicknamed ‘Crow Castle’ for its striking black exterior, is one of Japan’s most important original castles and a designated National Treasure, its five-tiered keep dating to the late 16th century and standing as one of the oldest surviving original keeps in the country. Unlike hilltop castles, it sits on flat land surrounded by a wide moat that mirrors the black-and-white keep, and the scene is especially memorable when framed by cherry blossoms in late April or lit up during seasonal night illuminations reflecting on the still water.

item.title: Chureito Pagoda: The Iconic Five-Storey Pagoda With Mount Fuji — Guide
item.description: Chureito Pagoda is a five-storey red pagoda set on a hillside above Fujiyoshida, reached by a climb of just under 400 steps, and frames one of Japan’s most iconic views: the vermilion pagoda in the foreground with Mount Fuji rising behind it across the town below. The scene is especially striking in spring when cherry blossoms surround the pagoda, and in autumn with coloured foliage, drawing photographers from around the world to what has become one of the most recognisable images of Japan.

item.title: Maruoka Castle: One of Japan's Oldest Surviving Castle Keeps — Guide
item.description: Maruoka Castle was built in 1576 and its keep is considered one of the oldest surviving original castle structures in Japan, having survived centuries of conflict, fire and the widespread castle demolitions of the Meiji era that destroyed many of the country’s original fortifications. Unlike the larger, more elaborate reconstructed castles found elsewhere in Japan, Maruoka’s modest, sturdy keep with its distinctive stone-tiled roof offers visitors a rare, authentic look at genuine Sengoku-period castle architecture, and the surrounding park is a popular local cherry blossom spot each spring.

item.title: Takada Castle Ruins: 4,000 Cherry Trees & Japan's Great Night Blossoms — Guide
item.description: Takada Castle, once home to a feudal lord and later a military garrison, survives today primarily as a moated park rather than a standing keep, but its roughly 4,000 cherry trees have earned it a place among Japan’s three great night cherry blossom viewing spots. Each spring, the annual Takada Cherry Blossom Festival illuminates the trees and their reflections in the surrounding moat, drawing large crowds for an evening spectacle that ranks among the most photographed cherry blossom scenes in the country.

item.title: Toyama Castle: The City's Reconstructed Landmark Keep — Guide
item.description: Toyama Castle, originally built in the 16th century and reconstructed in concrete in 1954 after the original structure was lost, stands at the centre of Toyama City in a pleasant park setting surrounded by a moat lined with cherry trees. The keep houses a small local history museum with displays on the castle and city’s past, and an observation level offers views over central Toyama, making it an easy, low-commitment stop for visitors exploring the city on foot.

item.title: Miharu Takizakura: Japan's 1,000-Year Weeping Cherry Tree — Guide
item.description: Miharu Takizakura — the ‘Miharu Waterfall Cherry’ — is an estimated 1,000-year-old weeping cherry tree, designated a National Natural Monument and ranked among Japan’s three great cherry trees. Its massive, gnarled trunk supports cascading branches that, in full bloom each April, pour down like a pink waterfall, drawing photographers and pilgrims from across Japan. During the roughly two-week blossom festival, the tree is illuminated after dark, creating an especially dramatic sight against the night sky.

item.title: Tsurugajo Castle, Aizu-Wakamatsu: A Samurai Stronghold Reborn — Guide
item.description: Tsurugajo Castle in Aizu-Wakamatsu is one of Japan’s most storied fortresses — the site of a month-long 1868 siege during the Boshin War, when Aizu samurai (including the teenage Byakkotai) made their last stand against imperial forces. The current five-storey keep, rebuilt in 1965 with a distinctive red-tile roof unique among Japanese castles, houses a museum on Aizu’s samurai history, and the surrounding park bursts into roughly 1,000 cherry trees each April.

item.title: Hirosaki Castle & Cherry Blossoms: Japan's Best Hanami — Guide
item.description: Hirosaki Castle in western Aomori holds one of only twelve original Edo-period keeps left in Japan — but it is most famous as the country’s greatest cherry blossom site. In late April some 2,600 trees erupt in bloom, and fallen petals blanket the moat into the legendary pink ‘hanaikada’ flower raft. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Park always open; keep ~9:00–17:00 Admission Park free; castle areas ~¥320 Time needed 1.

item.title: Kitakami Tenshochi: Iwate's Riverside Cherry Tunnel — Guide
item.description: Stretching two kilometres along the Kitakami River, Tenshochi Park is lined with 10,000 Yoshino cherry trees that form a blossoming tunnel each April. Rent a rowboat to drift beneath the overhanging branches, or ride the little steam train through the park. Blossoms reflected in the river with the distant Kitakami mountains make this one of Tohoku’s most beloved spring walks. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Kitakami, Iwate Hours Park always open; festival late Apr Admission Free (boat/train extra) Time needed 1.

item.title: Morioka Castle Ruins & Iwate Park: City Cherry Blossoms — Guide
item.description: Morioka Castle was one of Tohoku’s great fortresses. Only the stone walls remain, but they are spectacular — rising over the Nakatsu River with Iwate-san volcano framed behind. The surrounding Iwate Park (Morioka Castle Ruins Park) is the city’s finest cherry blossom spot, with over 300 trees. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours Park always open Admission Free Time needed About 1 hour Best time Late April (cherry blossoms) What to See Spectacular Edo-era stone walls above the river.

item.title: Morioka Cherry Blossoms: Late-Blooming Tohoku Sakura — Guide
item.description: Morioka’s cherry blossoms bloom two to three weeks later than Tokyo’s — in late April, Iwate Park (Morioka Castle ruins) erupts with over 300 trees against ancient stone walls, with snow-capped Mt. Iwate behind. Don’t miss the famous Ishiwari-zakura, a cherry tree growing straight out of a granite boulder in central Morioka. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Morioka, Iwate Hours Parks always open Admission Free Time needed 1.

item.title: Saishoin Five-Story Pagoda: Hirosaki's Elegant Landmark — Guide
item.description: The five-story pagoda of Saishoin temple in Hirosaki is an Important Cultural Property and one of the most beautiful in northern Japan. Built in the 17th century, its slender vermilion tiers are especially lovely framed by spring cherry blossoms. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Grounds daytime; ~9:00–16:30 Admission Free (grounds) Time needed 30–45 minutes Best time Spring (cherry blossoms) What to See The elegant 17th-century five-story pagoda, an Important Cultural Property.

item.title: Senshu Park & Kubota Castle: Akita City's Green Heart — Guide
item.description: Akita City’s Senshu Park occupies the site of Kubota Castle, former seat of the Satake clan, with a reconstructed turret offering city views. Its 840 cherry trees are among Tohoku’s finest, and the surrounding museum district includes the Tadao Ando-designed Akita Museum of Art, home to Foujita’s vast mural ‘Events in Akita’. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Akita City, Akita Hours Park always open; turret ~9:00–16:30 Admission Park free; turret small fee Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Chiba Castle Guide: Museum, Cherry Blossoms & Access
item.description: In the heart of Chiba City, Chiba Castle crowns the leafy Inohana hill where the powerful Chiba clan once ruled the region in the medieval era. The handsome white keep you see today is a modern reconstruction housing the Chiba City Folk Museum, which traces the clan’s history and local samurai culture. Surrounded by Inohana Park — one of the city’s best cherry-blossom spots — and close to the venerable Chiba Shrine, it makes an easy, pleasant half-day of history, greenery and city sightseeing right by central Chiba.

item.title: Izumi Nature Park Cherry Blossom Guide: Sakura & Access
item.description: When spring arrives in the rural Boso interior, Izumi Nature Park near Sosa becomes one of Chiba’s loveliest cherry-blossom (sakura) spots — a quiet expanse of ponds, woods and meadows where rows of cherry trees bloom alongside golden rapeseed flowers for a classic pink-and-yellow spring scene. Far from the city crowds, it’s a peaceful place for hanami picnics, gentle walks and birdwatching, and it pairs perfectly with the Isumi Railway, whose little trains roll through the same flower-filled countryside.

item.title: Odawara Castle & Hojo Festival Guide: What to See & Access
item.description: The castle town of Odawara, gateway to Hakone, was once the mighty stronghold of the Hojo clan who ruled much of eastern Japan until Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s famous siege in 1590. Today its handsomely reconstructed castle keep anchors a park of cherry trees and museums, and each spring the town celebrates its samurai past with the Hojo Godai Festival, when costumed warriors, princesses and musicians parade through the streets. Add a moat-side bloom of cherry blossoms, a hilltop view to the sea, and the town’s famous kamaboko fish cake, and Odawara makes a rewarding history stop on the way to Hakone.

item.title: Osaka Castle Guide: The Tower, Park & Best Times to Visit
item.description: Rising on its great stone base above a sea of green, Osaka Castle is the symbol of the city and its single most famous sight. The gleaming white-and-green keep, trimmed with golden tigers and crests, sits within a vast park ringed by massive stone walls and broad moats — a monument to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlord who unified Japan and built his power base here in the 16th century. Today the keep houses a modern museum, the top floor offers sweeping city views, and the surrounding park is one of Osaka’s best spots for cherry and plum blossom.

item.title: Osaka Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots & Timing
item.description: For about two weeks each spring, Osaka turns pink. Cherry blossom (sakura) season transforms the castle moats, riverbanks, and parks into clouds of blossom, and the city throws itself into hanami — flower-viewing picnics under the trees, by day and (lit up) by night. From the iconic combination of blossoms and Osaka Castle to the riverside tunnels of the Kema Sakuranomiya and the once-a-year Japan Mint passage, Osaka has some of the Kansai region’s best and liveliest cherry-blossom spots.

item.title: Philosopher's Path Guide: Kyoto's Most Beautiful Walk
item.description: The Philosopher’s Path (Tetsugaku-no-michi) is a stone-paved walking trail that follows a cherry-tree-lined canal through the quiet temple district of eastern Kyoto. Named for a famous philosophy professor who walked it daily in meditation on his way to Kyoto University, it strings together some of the city’s loveliest temples, shrines, cafés, and craft shops over about two gentle kilometres. In cherry-blossom season it becomes a tunnel of pink reflected in the water; in autumn, a corridor of red and gold.

item.title: Tokyo Cherry Blossom Guide: Best Hanami Spots, Timing & Etiquette
item.description: There is no week in the Japanese calendar more celebrated than sakura season. For about ten days each spring, Tokyo — a city of 14 million people — pivots its entire social life around sitting under trees. Friends, families, and colleagues converge on parks from early morning to claim prime spots, spread blue tarps, and spend the afternoon eating, drinking, and staring upward at a canopy of pale pink that will be completely gone in a week.

item.title: Matsumoto Castle: Complete Visitor Guide
item.description: Matsumoto Castle is the finest surviving original castle in Japan. Unlike the many concrete reconstructions found across the country, Matsumoto’s six-storey black-and-white keep has stood in its current form since the late 16th century — its heavy timbers, hand-plastered walls, and original stone foundations are the real thing. Set against the jagged silhouette of the Northern Japan Alps, with a mirror-surface moat reflecting its black towers, the castle creates a scene of architectural drama that ranks among the most photographed in all of Japan.

item.title: Aomori Events & Festivals: Nebuta, Hirosaki Cherry Blossoms & Hachinohe Emburi
item.description: Aomori Prefecture Events and Festivals Guide for International Visitors Aomori Prefecture, occupying Japan’s northernmost point on Honshu, hosts some of the nation’s most spectacular and unique festivals. From explosive summer celebrations to mystical winter rituals, these events offer international visitors authentic cultural experiences far removed from typical tourist circuits. 1. Aomori Nebuta Festival (August 2–7) Overview The Aomori Nebuta Festival ranks among Japan’s three greatest festivals (alongside Sendai Tanabata and Akita Kanto), drawing approximately three million spectators annually.
